altKeyTip: The post-quantum key each authority holds beside its classical one, in the alternative-key extensions of ITU-T X.509 (2019) clause 9.8. Every certificate the authority issues is then signed twice, and this service refuses one whose second signature is wrong or missing. "none" builds a classical-only authority, which a quantum-capable attacker can forge.
sigRightOne: (the right one for the key algorithm)
sigWeakProduct: [weak, on purpose — refused in product mode]
bcTip: Whether this certificate may act as a CA, and how many CAs may follow it. RFC 5280 requires it to be critical in a CA certificate.
bcCriticalTip: RFC 5280: MUST be critical in a CA certificate.
bcCaTip: This certificate may sign other certificates.
bcPathlenTip: How many further CA certificates may appear below this one. 0 means it may only sign leaves. Empty means unlimited.
kuTip: What the certified key may be used for. RFC 5280 says this SHOULD be critical.
ekuTip: The purposes this certificate is for. A TLS client refuses a server certificate without serverAuth; a server refuses a client certificate without clientAuth.
ekuCriticalTip: Marking this critical means a validator that does not recognise one of the OIDs must reject the certificate.
ekuExtraTip: For a purpose that is not one of the {n} above.
skidTip: The SHA-1 of this certificate’s public key, RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.2 method (1) — the same value every other implementation computes, so key identifiers match across tools.
akidTip: Identifies the ISSUER’s key, so a validator can find the right CA certificate when several share a subject.
akidIssuerSerialTip: Also name the issuer’s own issuer and serial number. Rarely needed, occasionally required.
sanTip: The names this certificate is for. For TLS this — not the Common Name — is what a client checks.
sanCriticalTip: Should be critical when the subject DN is empty, and only then.
sanSyntax: dns:example.com — ip:10.0.0.1 or ip:2001:db8::1 — email:user@example.com — uri:https://example.com/x — upn:user@EXAMPLE.COM — krb5:host/x@EXAMPLE.COM — rid:1.2.3.4 — dirname:CN=alt,O=Example — othername:{oid}:{der}.
ianTip: Alternative names for the issuer. Same syntax as subjectAltName.
ianSyntax: The same syntax as subjectAltName above.
cdpTip: Where to fetch the CRL that would revoke this certificate. NOTE that this service publishes none: the extension is a URL you are asserting, not a promise this mock keeps.
cdpUrlsTip: Where the CRL that would revoke this certificate is published.
freshestTip: Where to fetch the DELTA CRL. The same shape as cRLDistributionPoints and a different extension.
freshestUrlsTip: Where the delta CRL is published.
aiaTip: Where to reach the issuer: its OCSP responder, and a copy of its own certificate for a client that was sent an incomplete chain.
aiaSyntax: ocsp:{url}, caissuers:{url}, timestamping:{url}, carepository:{url}, or {oid}:{url} for a method this page does not name.
siaTip: Services offered by the SUBJECT of this certificate, rather than by its issuer.
siaSyntax: The same syntax as authorityInfoAccess above.
policiesTip: The policies this certificate was issued under, with the two qualifiers RFC 5280 defines.
policiesCriticalTip: Critical means a validator that cannot process the policy must reject the certificate.
policiesSyntax: {oid}, optionally followed by |cps={uri} and |notice={text}. 2.5.29.32.0 is anyPolicy.
mappingsTip: Declares that one policy OID in the issuer’s domain is equivalent to another in the subject’s. RFC 5280 says this SHOULD be critical, and it is.
policyConstraintsTip: Requires an explicit policy, or inhibits policy mapping, after a number of further certificates. RFC 5280: MUST be critical, and it is.
requireExplicitTip: How many further certificates may appear before an acceptable policy is required. Empty means it is not set.
inhibitMappingTip: How many further certificates may still map policies. Empty means it is not set.
nameConstraintsTip: Limits the names a CA below this one may certify — the extension that makes a private CA safe to trust. RFC 5280: MUST be critical, and only meaningful in a CA certificate.
nameConstraintsSyntax: "permit {name}" or "exclude {name}", using the subjectAltName syntax. An IP constraint takes a PREFIX (10.0.0.0/8): a name constraint’s iPAddress is the address followed by its mask, which is the one place a general name is not simply an address.
inhibitAnyTip: How many further certificates may still use the anyPolicy OID. RFC 5280: MUST be critical, and it is.
skipCertsTip: 0 means anyPolicy is not accepted below this certificate at all.
pkupTip: A validity period for the PRIVATE key that is shorter than the certificate’s — signatures made after it are not to be trusted, while the certificate goes on validating them.
pkupNotBeforeTip: When the private key may start signing. Encoded as a GeneralizedTime in UTC. Empty leaves it out.
pkupNotAfterTip: When the private key must stop signing — earlier than the certificate’s own notAfter, which goes on validating what was signed before it. Empty leaves it out.
tlsFeatureTip: The TLS extensions a server promises to support. 5 is status_request — "must-staple"; 17 is status_request_v2.
tlsFeatureNumbersTip: One TLS extension number per line.
ocspNocheckTip: Tells a validator not to check the revocation status of this certificate — correct on an OCSP responder’s own certificate and almost nowhere else.
nsCertTypeTip: A pre-RFC 5280 relic that some old appliances still read. Kept for the same reason SHA-1 is: this is where you find out.
nsCommentTip: A free-text comment some tools display when showing the certificate.
anyOtherTip: Any extension at all, by OID and base64 DER — including one this page has never heard of. Without this the extension set would be whatever this page happens to know about, which is not what a debugging tool is for.
customSyntax: {oid}|{critical}|{der}. The value is the DER of the extnValue’s contents, not the OCTET STRING wrapping it.
noCaYet: (no certificate authority in this realm yet)
profileNote: The profile sets the extensions below to what that kind of certificate normally carries; every one of them is then editable, which is the point — issuing the certificate that is wrong in exactly one way is how you find out what refuses it and what does not. Pressing Apply the profile rewrites the extension boxes, because on this console the form IS the extension set: a profile that changed what gets issued and not what is shown would be a page that lies about what it is about to do.
profileNoteTitle: What the profile does, and why every field it sets stays editable
profileTip: What kind of certificate this is. It sets the default extensions, the default validity, and whether it is self-signed.
applyProfileTip: Rewrite the extension boxes, the default validity and the profile's Common Name from the profile chosen beside this button. Nothing is issued and a name you typed is kept.
selfSignedNote: {label} is SELF-SIGNED, so the key pair below signs its own certificate and Signed by is ignored. A "root" signed by something else is an intermediate.
signedByTip: The certificate authority that signs this certificate. Only authorities whose private key is still in this service are listed — one whose key was never kept cannot sign. The three tiers come from the hierarchy above; anything else is a CA issued from this pane.
approachTip: Which of the three ways this certificate carries post-quantum cryptography. It filters the Key Algorithm list beside this column and narrows the Signature Algorithm below; Hybrid additionally uses the alternative key pair, which goes into the X.509 (2019) alternative-signature extensions.
applyApproachTip: Redraw the two algorithm menus for the approach chosen beside this button. It is the same button as the one above it: with no script on this console, narrowing a menu is a round trip.
sigAlgTipSigner: The algorithm the ISSUER signs with. The list is what the signing key can actually produce — it is {signer} — because an RSA key cannot make an ECDSA signature and offering it produces a Web Crypto error that names neither.
sigAlgTip: The algorithm the ISSUER signs with. The list is what the signing key can actually produce because an RSA key cannot make an ECDSA signature and offering it produces a Web Crypto error that names neither.
sigRightOneSigning: (the right one for the signing key)
serialTip: Hex, and editable. A random 128-bit positive serial is filled in for you and a fresh one replaces it after every issue — that is what the CA/Browser Forum requires, and what makes a collision on the signed bytes impractical to arrange. Cleared, one is generated at issue time anyway.
validityYearsTip: Counted from Not Before, and used only when Not After below is empty. The profile sets it — 20 for a root, 10 for an intermediate, 5 for an issuing CA, 1 for a leaf.
notBeforeTip: Optional — empty means the moment the button is pressed. Anything Date can read; what is encoded is the instant, in UTC. A date at or after 2050 is encoded as a GeneralizedTime, as RFC 5280 requires — a UTCTime there is read as 1950, i.e. a certificate that expired seventy years ago.
notAfterTip: Optional — empty means Not Before plus the validity in years beside it.
keyPairNote: The key pair the next certificate certifies — and, for a self-signed profile, the key that signs it. It is generated here, in this service, which is the one place this page differs in kind from the debugger's: that page generates in the browser because its whole claim is that the key never leaves it, and this one holds the certificate authority, so the key belongs in the process that signs. It is the same module either way (common/vendored/key_material.js), so the algorithms, the PEM/JWK conversion and the keystore formats are identical rather than similar.
slowWarn: {families} key generation takes up to a second and it runs on this thread. This process owns six listener families on one thread, so while a key like that is being made this service answers nobody — not the next HTTP caller, not the KDC on port 88, not the LDAP socket. The primitive is native (node's OpenSSL since #363), and the SLH-DSA s parameter sets are slow by design even so. In dispatch mode the console holds affinity to a request worker, so the stall is that worker's rather than the listener's.
slowWarnTitle: One algorithm family is slow, and the cost is real
keyAlgTip: The algorithm and parameters of the key pair. RSA sizes are the modulus; the EC entries are the NIST curves; Ed25519 is the only Edwards curve here. The list is narrowed by the Cryptographic Approach in the column beside this one.
showJwkTip: Show the key pair as JWK instead of PEM. The conversion is key material only — the same key either way. A POST-QUANTUM pair is shown as PEM whatever this says, because these two boxes are also the INPUT for a reuse and a round trip through a representation this encoder cannot read back would lose the key.
generateTip: Generate a key pair into the two boxes below WITHOUT issuing anything, and tick nothing. It exists because generating a post-quantum pair takes seconds: making one and then issuing four certificates from it is the difference between a page somebody can use and one they cannot.
reuseKeyTip: Certify the key pair already in the boxes below instead of generating a new one — a CA re-issuing its own certificate, or the pair the store's "Use this key pair" button loaded here. Cleared, every issue starts from a fresh pair.
saveKeys: keep the private key in this service
saveKeysTip: THIS IS THE ONE CONTROL ON THIS PANE THAT MEANS SOMETHING DIFFERENT FROM THE DEBUGGER'S. There it decides whether the private key is written to the browser's localStorage; here there is no browser store, so it decides whether the issued object keeps its private key in this realm's keystore row. Cleared, the certificate and the public key are stored and the private half is discarded the moment the reply is written — so the object can be inspected and used as a trust anchor, and can never sign again or be exported.
privateKeyTip: PKCS#8 PEM (or JWK). It signs, and for a CA it goes on signing long after this certificate was issued. There is no Copy button because this console has no script; the box selects.
publicKeyTip: SubjectPublicKeyInfo PEM (or JWK). This is what the certificate certifies.
genCsr: generate a CSR when the certificate is issued
genCsrTip: Also build the PKCS#10 certification request this key pair and subject would have sent to an external authority. It is FOR REFERENCE: this page signs the certificate itself, so nothing here consumes the CSR — it is what you would paste into a CA that will not take a certificate you made yourself. The signature on it is by the private key above, which is the proof of possession that lets an authority certify a key it has never seen.
csrTip: The certification request for the key pair and subject above, built from the SAME inputs the certificate was — a request assembled from a second reading of the form would differ in ways nobody could see. THREE EXTENSIONS TRAVEL AND THE REST DO NOT: key usage, extended key usage, basic constraints and subjectAltName. subjectKeyIdentifier and authorityKeyIdentifier are the ISSUER's to compute, and a requester asserting them is asking a CA to certify its own arithmetic. Empty until the box above is ticked and something is issued.
altPairNote: ITU-T X.509 (2019) clause 9.8 adds three non-critical extensions that mirror three fields of the certificate: subjectAltPublicKeyInfo (2.5.29.72), altSignatureAlgorithm (2.5.29.73) and altSignatureValue (2.5.29.74). A certificate carrying them is signed twice, with two keys, and a validator that has never heard of the extensions sees an ordinary certificate and accepts it — which is the entire point. The alternative signature does not cover the whole TBSCertificate: it covers the preTBSCertificate, which is the TBSCertificate with the signature field removed and without the altSignatureValue extension. These boxes are used only when the Cryptographic Approach is Hybrid; for a self-signed certificate this pair makes the second signature, and for an issued one the ISSUER's alternative key does and this one is only certified.
altPairNoteTitle: What the second key is for
altAlgTip: Where the post-quantum half of a hybrid certificate goes, so the list is the post-quantum algorithms that can sign — a hybrid certificate whose second key is also RSA is a certificate signed twice by the same century.
altReuseTip: Certify the alternative pair already in the boxes instead of generating a new one.
generateAltTip: Generate the alternative key pair now. Issuing under the Hybrid approach generates one anyway if these boxes are empty.
altPrivateKeyTip: PKCS#8 PEM. For a self-signed certificate this is what signs the preTBSCertificate; for an issued one the issuer's own alternative private key is used instead and this one is only certified.
altPublicKeyTip: SubjectPublicKeyInfo PEM. This is what goes into the subjectAltPublicKeyInfo extension.
exportNote: Writes out the key pair of the object SELECTED in the store below, or the pair in the boxes above when nothing is selected. It is the same export /admin/keys uses — common/vendored/key_material.js — so a .p12 from here and one from that page import identically into keytool, OpenSSL, Windows and macOS. It needs Admin Write, like every other door here that hands over a private key: reading this console needs Admin Read, and taking a key out of it needs the other role.
ksFormatTip: PEM: the private key and public key (and the chain, if an object is selected) in one file. DER: two binary files, of which the PRIVATE one is sent — this service will not take a zip dependency to send two, and the public half comes out of the private one with one openssl command. JWK: a JWK set. PKCS#12: a password-protected .p12 holding the key and its certificate chain.
ksPasswordTip: Required for PKCS#12. For PEM and DER it encrypts the private key as a PBES2 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo; for JWK it wraps the set in a PBES2 JWE. Left empty, the private key is written out in the clear.
includeChainTip: Put the selected object's whole certificate chain in the file, which is what makes a PKCS#12 importable as an identity rather than as a bare key.
downloadTip: Download the key pair. This button sends the same form to the export, whose answer is the FILE the browser saves rather than a page.
dnCnTip: commonName (2.5.4.3) — what this certificate is called. The profile fills it in and replaces its own default when the profile changes, but never a name you typed. For a TLS server the name a client actually checks is in subjectAltName, not here.
dnOTip: organizationName (2.5.4.10) — who the subject belongs to. It is filled from pki.organisation, which is what the hierarchy above carries, because two certificates from one realm reading O=Example and O=sts are two organisations as far as a path validator is concerned.
dnOuTip: organizationalUnitName (2.5.4.11) — the division within the organization. Repeat it by adding OU=… lines to Further attributes below; a DN may carry several.
dnStTip: stateOrProvinceName (2.5.4.8) — spelled out rather than abbreviated, which is what the CA/Browser Forum asks for.
dnCTip: countryName (2.5.4.6). Two letters, encoded as a PrintableString — a country encoded as UTF8String parses perfectly and is refused by several validators.
dnEmailTip: emailAddress (1.2.840.113549.1.9.1) — a legacy PKCS#9 attribute in the DN. S/MIME clients read the rfc822Name in subjectAltName instead, so an address here alone is decorative.
dnDcTip: domainComponent (0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.25) — one label of a DNS name, as Active Directory writes a DN (DC=example, DC=com). Add further DC=… lines to Further attributes below, in order.
dnUidTip: userId (0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.1) — the account name, as a directory holds it.
dnSerialTip: The DN attribute called serialNumber (2.5.4.5). Nothing to do with the certificate's serial number in the first column.
dnOrderNote: Written in the order shown — a Name is an ordered RDNSequence, and a reordered DN is a different name that chains to nothing. For a TLS server, note that the name a client checks is in subjectAltName and not here: every current browser ignores the Common Name entirely.
dnOrderNoteTitle: Why the order matters, and where a TLS name really lives
dnExtra: Further attributes (one NAME=value or OID=value per line)
dnExtraTip: Appended in order. Recognised names include SN, GN, title, description, businessCategory, postalCode, STREET, initials, pseudonym, dnQualifier, generationQualifier and the three EV jurisdiction attributes; anything else is taken as an OID.
storeEmpty: Nothing has been issued from the pane above in this realm. What is issued here is kept in the same keystore row as the hierarchy — sealed under the same key-encryption key, gone with the realm, and in development mode gone with the process, which is the rule the signing key already follows.
noCannotSign: no — it cannot sign or be exported
useKeyTip: Load this key pair into the boxes above and tick "reuse the key pair below", so the next issue certifies THIS key — a CA renewing its own certificate. Everything else on the form is kept.
removeObjectTip: Remove this object. Anything it issued is KEPT — those certificates are still valid documents — and will say that their issuer is missing.
clearStoreTip: Discard every key pair and certificate this pane has issued in this realm. The hierarchy above is NOT touched.
paneIntro: This is the parent project’s PKI / X.509 workflow, on the server. Build a certificate authority and issue the leaf certificates any of them can sign: TLS server, TLS client for mutual authentication, code signing, S/MIME, OCSP responder, time stamping, smartcard logon and Kerberos PKINIT. Every X.509v3 extension RFC 5280 defines is below, plus the ones in common use that it does not, plus anything at all by OID. The encoder is common/vendored/x509.js, that project’s own PKI code byte-identical, so a certificate issued here and one issued there are built by one encoder.
paneWhere: What is different is where the computation happens. That page runs Web Crypto in your browser and filters its menus as you change them; this console is script-src 'none', so every choice is a form field and every computation is here. The two Apply buttons are what that costs: narrowing a menu or rewriting the extension boxes from a profile is a round trip rather than an event handler.
paneAsserting: A cRLDistributionPoints or an authorityInfoAccess you type below is a URL you are ASSERTING, and this pane keeps no promise about it. That was true of every address on this page until 2026-09-11 and it is still true of every address you type — what changed is that the certificates this service issues itself now name addresses it really answers: each authority signs a CRL and runs an OCSP responder, and anything issued from one of them can be revoked in the pane below. An object minted here from an authority whose key is in this process is in that register too. One typed at a URL of your own is not, and nothing here will pretend otherwise.
paneIntroTitle: What this pane is, and how it differs from the page it is modelled on
extensionsNote: Every extension RFC 5280 defines, plus the ones in common use that it does not, plus anything at all by OID. The critical flag is separately settable on each: a validator must reject a certificate carrying a critical extension it does not understand, so making the wrong one critical is a good way to find out what your stack actually implements. Four of them are fixed critical because RFC 5280 says MUST or SHOULD and a box that could clear it would produce a certificate nothing profiles — policyMappings, policyConstraints and inhibitAnyPolicy.
extensionsNoteTitle: Which extensions are here, and what the critical flag costs
issueTip: Generate a key pair unless "reuse the key pair below" is ticked, build the certificate, sign it, and keep both in the store below.
storeNote: Everything issued from the pane above, in this realm, newest first. Select a row to export it or to load its key pair back into the form. At most {n} are kept: past that the oldest goes and the reply says so, because every one of these is sealed, written to the store and pushed to every request worker when it changes.
noRoot: This service has no Root CA. It is built at startup unless pki.autoBuild is off, so seeing this means either that setting is off or the build failed — the startup log says which. Every key this service holds is self-signed until there is one, which is what this service did before 2026-09-11.
noIntermediate: This scope has no Intermediate CA. Build it below.
pinExpired: The certificate of the pinned {unit} signing key {kid} has expired ({when}), and the key still signs. Relying parties that check it refuse what it signs.
pinExpiring: The certificate of the pinned {unit} signing key {kid} expires on {when} ({n} day(s)).
pinNeverRotated: A pinned key is never rotated: pin a renewed key pair, or unpin it below.
pinWarnTitle: A pinned signing key is near the end of its life
unpinTip: Stop signing with this key. The key this service generated signs again at once — it was published all along — and this one stays published, verifying what it signed, through the unit's grace. A signing-key-rotated event is sent.
pinnedOn: This realm signs with pinned keys (pki.pinnedSigners): a key pair pinned into a jose or xml slot below is published at once and signs for that algorithm after pki.pinnedSignerLeadMinutes ({n} minute(s)). Its lifecycle is yours: it is never rotated, and it ends when its certificate does.
pinnedOff: Off in this realm (pki.pinnedSigners): the realm signs with the keys it generates, and a pin into a slot it signs from is refused. Turn the setting on to sign with a key pair of your own — and take over its lifecycle.
nothingPinned: Nothing is pinned in this realm.
branchKeyAlgTip: The key algorithm every CA in this branch is generated with. The Root keeps its own — a branch built with a different algorithm from the Root is perfectly legal, and the SIGNATURE on each tier is the one its issuer can produce whatever this says.
buildBranchTip: Replace this branch: a new Intermediate CA and a new Issuing CA for every use case under it. The Root is NOT touched — every other scope hangs from it. Everything this branch had issued chains to nothing the moment this returns, which is why the certificates under it are re-minted in the same act.
reissueTip: Generate a new key pair for this Issuing CA and re-issue it from this scope’s Intermediate, then re-certify everything that hung under it. The other use cases are untouched, which is the whole reason each has an authority of its own.
renewTip: Re-issue the certificates under this CA from the same authority, with fresh serials and a fresh validity window. The KEYS are untouched — this is a renewal, not a regeneration, so nothing that verifies against the published keys stops verifying.
useOwnPairNote: Replace what this service generated for one SLOT with a key pair of your own. With no certificate this service issues one from the authority above, so your key chains to this service’s Root exactly as a generated one would; with a certificate, the pair is used as you supplied it and chains wherever that certificate chains.
chainPem: Its chain, leaf’s issuer first (PEM, optional; published as the x5c of a pinned signing key)
useAsIssuing: Use this as the Issuing CA
rootWarn: Replacing the Root replaces the trust anchor for the whole service. Every scope’s Intermediate is signed by it, so rebuilding it here re-signs all of them in the same act — and anything that was trusting the old Root stops trusting this service until it is given the new one. That is the cost of one anchor covering everything, and it is the reason the button says what it does.
rootWarnTitle: This replaces the anchor everything hangs from
importRoot: Import a Root of your own
importRootNote: Paste a CA certificate and its private key and this service will hang every Intermediate from it instead of building one — so the whole tree chains to your own corporate authority and a relying party that already trusts it needs nothing new. The key is stored exactly as this service stores its own: in the realm keystore row, sealed under the key-encryption key wherever that key outlives the process, and in the clear in development mode where it does not.
useAsRoot: Use this as the Root CA
coverageEvery: Every signing key pair this service generates is a leaf of this tree, the post-quantum ones included (2026-09-13). A realm’s eleven post-quantum signing keys — ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and the six composites — are issued from that realm’s own JOSE signing Issuing CA as they are made, and each is refused in any other realm by the Intermediate boundary every leaf here is held to. The keys are still generated and signed with by common/pq_jose.js, this service’s own reading of those constructions: only the PUBLIC key reaches the certificate encoder, and a signature from one reading is checked to verify under the other against the certificate. The JWKS is unchanged — they are still published as AKP JWKs. An ML-DSA listener certificate (tls.certificateAlgorithms) is a leaf of the TLS listeners Issuing CA beside the RSA one.
coverageOutside: Two keys stay outside, by what they are. The SPIFFE JWT authority has no certificate to issue — a JWT-SVID is verified against a bare key in the bundle — and the OpenID4VCI request-encryption key only DECRYPTS and is trusted because a wallet read it out of the issuer’s own metadata.
coverageSpiffe: The SPIFFE X.509 authority used to be on this list and is under this Root (2026-09-11) — it is the SPIFFE authority Issuing CA in each realm's branch above, and every X509-SVID this service mints is a leaf of it. It is the one Issuing CA in this hierarchy with pathLen: 1 rather than 0, because NewDownstreamX509CA on the SPIRE Server API asks it for a CA and not a leaf; the realm Intermediate above it is widened to 2 to match, and common/pki.js derives the second from the first so the two cannot drift.
coverageSpiffeAfter: reports which authority each realm is actually using — a realm with no branch built still falls back to a self-signed one and says so.
issuedNothing: This authority has issued nothing this process can still see.
issuedNoMatch: No certificate this authority issued matches the search above.
releaseHoldTip: Take this serial off the list. Only a `certificateHold` can be released — every other reason is permanent under RFC 5280, because a validator is entitled to cache a permanent revocation for as long as the CRL it read says it is fresh.
revokeTip: Put this serial on {label}’s revocation list. It changes nothing about who HOLDS the key — what it changes is what this service’s CRL and OCSP responder say about this serial from now on.
orphansNote: {n} serial(s) on this list name a certificate this process no longer holds a record of. That is the ORDINARY case rather than an error: a certificate superseded by a rotation is revoked and then REPLACED in the register, so the old serial stays on the list with nothing left to point at. RFC 5280 does not ask a CA to still hold what it signed in order to revoke it — and a validator checking one of these is checking exactly the certificate it was meant to.
searchOrphansPlaceholder: a serial, part of a subject, a reason
orphansNoMatch: No revoked serial here matches the search.
orphansTitle: {n} revoked serial(s) with no certificate left to show
authorityCounts: {issued} issued, {revoked} revoked. A client reads this authority’s answer at {http} (HTTP), {ldap} (LDAP) or {ocsp} (OCSP). Every certificate this authority signs names all three inside itself.
searchIssuedPlaceholder: a serial, part of a subject or a name
noAuthorityToRevoke: There is no certificate authority in the {realm} realm or on the process branch yet, so there is nothing here to revoke and no list to publish. Build one above. Another realm’s authorities are not counted — they are revoked in that realm.
revokeByIssuer: A revocation is made BY AN ISSUER, which is why this pane is organised by authority rather than by certificate: a serial number is unique only within one issuer, so revoke serial 4f2a is not a question this service can answer. It is also why there is one CRL and one OCSP responder per authority rather than one per realm — a list per realm would be a document with no valid issuer, and nothing could sign it.
revokeNotTakeOff: This is not the Take the key pair off control in the Applications table, and the difference matters. That one changes an application’s directory entry, so this service stops ACCEPTING what the key signs — and the certificate goes on chaining to this realm’s Root for anybody who only checks the chain. This one changes what the CRL and the OCSP responder SAY, and changes nothing about who holds what. An operator dealing with a compromised key pair almost certainly wants both, and they are two buttons because they are two acts with different blast radii.
revokePublishes: This service PUBLISHES revocation and cannot make anybody consult it. A certificate revoked here goes on the list and its responder answers revoked; whether that stops anything depends entirely on the relying party. That is true of every certificate authority there has ever been, and it is exactly why a client author would point their stack at this one. This service does not consult it either — a client certificate presented on the main port or on LDAPS 636 is checked against the anchors on /tls/trust and no CRL is fetched for it, so a certificate revoked here still gets in here.
revokeWhatTitle: What revoking here does, and the three things it does not do
rotationRevokes: Most entries on these lists were not put there by hand. Every rotation revokes what it replaced, as superseded: reissuing a use case’s Issuing CA puts every leaf that CA had signed on its own list and puts the replaced CA on the Intermediate’s, and replacing the Root does the same one tier up. That is what makes the lists worth reading — a service where only hand-revocations appeared would publish an empty CRL for ever while quietly leaving superseded certificates chaining.
crlOnDemand: A CRL is built and signed on demand rather than cached, so thisUpdate is always now and a revocation is visible to the next fetch. pki.crlLifetimeMinutes is {n} minute(s), which is what nextUpdate and the HTTP cache header both say.
directoryCopyOn: The directory copy under ou=crl is republished as the list changes.
directoryCopyOff: The directory copy under ou=crl is OFF (pki.publishCrlToDirectory), so the ldap:// address inside these certificates resolve to nothing.
rotationTitle: Why these lists are not empty, and how fresh they are
reasonsNote: RFC 5280 section 5.3.1 defines eleven values and this service offers nine. 7 is unused and has never meant anything; removeFromCRL is a delta-CRL verb rather than a reason, and this service publishes no delta CRLs, so offering it would be a control that could never be honoured.
reasonsTitle: The nine reasons, and the two that are deliberately missing
searchApplicationsPlaceholder: an identifier, a profile, a handle or an issuer
searchPeoplePlaceholder: a username, a handle or an issuer
whatCa: This page builds a certificate authority for this trust realm — a Root CA, an Intermediate CA and an Issuing CA — and issues signing key pairs from the bottom of it to applications. It exists because of RFC 7521 and RFC 7523: an application can authenticate to the token endpoint, or present an authorization grant, with a signed assertion instead of a shared secret — and a signing key nobody vouched for is a key an operator has to move by hand.
whatAllThree: All three tiers are built in one act, or none is. A trust chain is only worth anything whole: an Issuing CA with no Intermediate above it is a two-tier chain wearing a three-tier name, and a half-built hierarchy is exactly the state in which somebody issues a certificate that verifies here and nowhere else.
whatPerRealm: It is per realm. A trust realm is a logical identity service with its own signing key and its own applications; a CA shared across realms would be one authority vouching for several services, which is the one thing a realm boundary exists to prevent. This page shows the {realm} realm.
whatEncoder: The encoder is common/vendored/x509.js — the parent project’s own PKI code, byte-identical, the same one behind its PKI / X.509 workflow page. So a certificate issued here and one issued there are built by one encoder, and a difference between them is a difference in the arguments rather than in two implementations that drifted.
publishedNotEnforced: Revocation here is PUBLISHED and never ENFORCED.
limitsTitle: What this certificate authority does not do
replacesWarn: A hierarchy already exists. Building again replaces it, and every certificate issued from the old one chains to nothing the moment it does — this service keeps no copy of what it issued, so none of them can be listed here.
issueToApplication: Issue a signing key pair to an application
issueWritesTip: The key pair is generated here, signed by the Issuing CA, and written onto that application’s entry. WHICH attributes depends on the profile: RFC 7523 writes seven — oauthAssertionPrivateKey, oauthAssertionCertificate, oauthAssertionCertificateChain, oauthAssertionJwks, oauthAssertionKid, oauthAssertionExpiresAt and oauthAssertionKeySource — and RFC 7522 writes six under oauthSamlAssertion*, with no JWKS among them because SAML has none: what a party registers for that profile is a certificate. They are separate key pairs and an application may hold both; neither can sign for the other’s profile, and taking one off leaves the other working. This service keeps NO second copy of the private key — the entry is where it lives, and it is SEALED there: AES-256-GCM under the same key-encryption key as the certificate authority above, wherever that key outlives the process. A directory dump, an ldif file, a database row or a backup holds ciphertext; this console and /admin-api open it for you, because the seal protects the store rather than the page you collect the key from. In development mode it is written in the clear, where the key-encryption key would not survive the restart the entry does. Issuing again replaces what is there.
nothingToIssue: There is no certificate authority in this realm yet, so there is nothing to issue from. Build one above.
issueToPerson: Issue a signing key pair to a person
personKeyTip: RFC 7523 section 2.1 does not say the issuer of an assertion has to be an application. Claim 1 asks only that iss be “a unique identifier for the JWT issuer”, and claim 2 says the sub of an authorization grant “typically identifies an authorized accessor or resource owner”. So a person holding a key of their own, signing this is me, issue a token for me, is the profile read literally — and it is the shape a client author most often wants to exercise: no browser, no password, a signature and an access token. RFC 7522 reads the same way for a SAML <Issuer>. This writes stsAssertion* for the JWT profile or stsSamlAssertion* for the SAML one onto that person’s entry — two sets sharing no name, so neither key pair signs for the other — with the private half sealed exactly as an application’s is. The person’s own page under /admin/users draws both, and replaces either with an uploaded certificate.
personOnlyThemselves: A person’s assertion may only be about themselves. The iss and the sub must name the same person, and one naming anybody else is refused — a key issued to one resource owner is that person’s credential rather than permission to speak for the others, and without the rule anybody given a key here could obtain a token as anybody in this realm. A party that may assert about other people is an APPLICATION with the issuer declared on it as oauthAssertionIssuer (or oauthSamlAssertionIssuer), which is a decision an operator makes deliberately. That is the whole difference between the two controls.
personShownOnce: The private key is shown once. It comes back on the page this form posts to and there is no second door to it: it is sealed on the entry and nothing here opens it. An application’s is different because /admin/applications already opens that one, and a console page that printed a person’s private key on every visit would be a worse answer than this.
personWarnTitle: Two things to know before you press it
noDirectory: This process has no directory, so nobody can hold an assertion key pair and an assertion naming a person as its issuer is refused for want of a registered issuer.
nobodyHolds: Nobody in this realm holds an assertion key pair.
noApplicationMatches: No application row matches the search.
noIssuerDeclared: none — it can authenticate, and cannot present an authorization grant
noApplicationHolds: No application in this realm holds a key pair issued here, and none declares an assertion issuer.
twoActsIntro: Holding a key pair and being trusted to assert are two different things, and this table shows both because an application commonly has one and not the other.
twoActsKeyPair: A key pair lets an application sign. That is all RFC 7523 section 2.2 needs — client authentication, where the assertion says who is calling — so an application with a key pair and no declared issuer can already authenticate at the token endpoint with private_key_jwt.
twoActsIssuer: A declared iss (oauthAssertionIssuer, set on the application’s own page) is what section 2.1 needs — the authorization grant, where the assertion says who the token is for. That grant has no browser, no password and no consent step in it, so the signature is the whole of its security: this service will not accept one from an issuer nobody declared, and oauth2.jwtBearerRequireRegisteredIssuer is on by default for the same reason federation refuses by default.
twoActsSelf: An assertion a client issues about itself needs no declaration: its iss is its own client_id, and that lookup already succeeds.
twoActsSaml: RFC 7522 is the same two acts over a SAML 2.0 assertion, with its own key pair and its own declaration (oauthSamlAssertionIssuer). The two profiles are kept apart deliberately: an application trusted to assert as a JWT has not thereby been trusted to assert as SAML, and the key pairs cannot stand in for one another. There is one further difference, and it is the only place this service is stricter for SAML: a JWT assertion may carry its certificate chain in x5c and be accepted because the chain reaches this realm’s Root, and a SAML assertion may not. A chain proves the realm issued a key; the URI subjectAltName in the leaf says who to, and the JWT grant reads it for exactly one purpose — holding a PERSON to asserting about themselves — rather than binding an application. So a chain still says nothing usable about which application holds a key, and accepting one here would let an application’s RFC 7523 leaf sign a SAML assertion, which is exactly the crossing the two key pairs exist to prevent.
twoActsTitle: A key pair is not a trust decision
treeOneRoot: One Root CA for the whole service, an Intermediate CA per scope, and an Issuing CA for each use case under it. Every key pair this service generates is a leaf of this tree — the signing keys of every realm, and the certificate the main port and LDAPS 636 serve — so an operator installs ONE anchor and it covers both of those sockets and every token this service signs.
treeRealmShares: A realm shares the Root and has an Intermediate of its own, and that is where the realm boundary is: with one Root, “this chains to our Root” is true of every realm’s certificates, so a path is checked against this realm’s own Intermediate instead. A certificate issued in one realm still does not verify in another.
treeDrawn: What is drawn below is the {realm} realm’s, and only that. The Root, because every realm hangs from it; the process branch, because the TLS and SPIFFE authorities certify sockets every realm answers on; and this realm’s own Intermediate with its Issuing CAs. Another realm’s branch is not here and cannot be edited from here — switch realms to reach it, which is how every other setting on this console already works. GET /admin-api/pki answers exactly this, in whichever realm it is reached in.
treeAutoBuild: It is built at startup (pki.autoBuild). Turning that off is how this service behaves as it did before 2026-09-11: nothing is built until Build is pressed and every key carries the self-signed certificate it was born with.
treeTitle: What this tree is, and where the realm boundary went
threeTierNote: The Root, this realm’s Intermediate and its application assertion Issuing CA — which is what GET /admin-api/pki has always answered and what RFC 7523 needs. The other Issuing CAs are in the tree above.
